title: The Prompt Is Still a Punch Card - Ted Johnson, JoinIn AI

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is AI interface design and UX, reframing prompting as an inadequate batch protocol and advocating participatory interfaces that remove human burdens. The talk addresses AI interface design broadly without being tied to a specific application vertical. The talk is a design-philosophy argument about envisioning better AI interfaces, not a production or deployment discussion. Conceptual frameworks and historical analogies are accessible to a general audience while offering depth for practitioners. The content is a 20-minute conference presentation with slides and live demonstrations. Arguments are supported by product demonstrations and practitioner experience rather than controlled experiments.

summary: Ted Johnson reframes AI as an interface technology, not only an intelligence technology. Over a 25-year career building enterprise software and collaboration systems, he observed a persistent mismatch between rising model capability and flat interface design. He introduces three foundational concepts. The channel is the physical transport carrying intent—keyboard, microphone, screen, punch card, or prompt box. Channels differ in signal type but bandwidth is not the same as machine understanding. Expression measures how much of what you mean the interface lets through; computing progressed from assembly opcodes through shell commands to programming languages, each a fixed vocabulary, until natural language blew the menu open. Protocol—the rules and shape of interaction—is where Johnson locates the core problem. Channels stayed the same, expression exploded with LLMs, but the protocol remained batch. Punch-card batch meant encoding a complete request in advance, submitting, waiting, reading output, finding errors, and resubmitting. Prompting follows the same pattern. Speed improvements shrank wait time but created an illusion of interactivity; shorter batch is still batch. Prompt engineering is merely rules for packaging batch. The human still does all contextual work: selecting context, choosing timing, noticing ambiguity, repairing output. When results disappoint, people blame themselves, but Johnson insists the mismatch is the interface, not the user. He demonstrates participatory alternatives. Nvidia's Personal Plex handles interruptions, yields, picks threads back up, and backchannels naturally. A multi-person business meeting scenario shows AI tracking speakers, labeling statements as questions or proposals, resolving scope objectives, capturing decisions, and choosing its moment to act—all without anyone writing or submitting a prompt. Johnson's mindset shift: stop picturing AI as a smarter machine behind prompts and start seeing intelligence as something that can remove interface constraints. For 75 years humans adapted to the machine's syntax, forms, timing, and batch. The design question becomes: what burden are we still putting on humans only because the machine used to be too limited to carry it? The answer isn't always chat, voice, or markdown—it's the affordances humans already use: a question, pause, sketch, checklist, quiet aside, or saying nothing. Computing has been about improving how humans encode intent for machines; each step carried old constraints forward as translation, precision, context, and repair taxes. AI is the chance to put those down by making computers more fluent with us.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: AI should be understood as an interface technology, not only an intelligence technology.
Three concepts frame the problem: channel (physical transport), expression (range of meaning carried), and protocol (rules of interaction).
Channels stayed the same and expression exploded with LLMs, but the protocol remained batch—identical to the punch-card era.
Prompt engineering is a set of rules for packaging batch, not a genuine advance in interaction design.
The core design question: what burden are we still putting on humans only because the machine used to be too limited to carry that burden itself?
The right interface answer is the affordances humans already use with each other—a question, pause, sketch, checklist, quiet aside, or saying nothing—not always chat, voice, or markdown.
For 75 years, humans adapted to the machine; every computing step carried old constraints forward as translation, precision, context, and repair taxes.
Participatory interfaces can track speakers, resolve objectives, capture decisions, and choose moments to act without anyone submitting a prompt.
Users wrongly blame themselves for poor AI results; the mismatch is the interface, not the user.
When you take the encoding burden off people, friction disappears and adoption follows.

sections.title: Opening: Making Prompting Strange Again
sections.summary: Johnson opens by noting the familiar act of typing a request into a box and waiting, then states his goal: to make prompting feel unfamiliar and strange again over the next 20 minutes.

sections.title: Background and Roadmap
sections.summary: Johnson introduces his 25-year career and his observation that AI feels unnatural to use, posing the question of why we still have to learn AI. He outlines the talk: three key concepts (channel, expression, protocol), the prompt as punch card, examples of interface progress, and practical advice.

sections.title: The Keyboard and the Concept of Channel
sections.summary: Johnson traces the keyboard to an arbitrary 1860s design under constraints that no longer exist, inherited and unnoticed. He defines channel as the medium an interface gives you to work in—keyboard, microphone, screen, punch card, prompt box—each carrying different signal types. Channel bandwidth is not the same as machine understanding.

sections.title: Expression: From Opcodes to Natural Language
sections.summary: Johnson defines expression as how much of what you mean the interface lets through. Computing progressed from assembly opcodes through shell commands to programming languages, each a fixed vocabulary. Natural language blew the menu open, enabling rich, complete human expression for the first time.

sections.title: Protocol: The Prompt as Punch Card
sections.summary: Johnson identifies protocol as the dimension that has not kept up. Batch processing—from punch cards to prompting—requires packaging a complete request in advance, submitting, waiting, and retrying. Speed shrank wait times but did not change the protocol. Prompt engineering is merely rules for packaging batch. The punch-card protocol originated from weaving looms and AI inherited it by default.

sections.title: The Mismatch and User Self-Blame
sections.summary: Model capacity curves upward while interface protocol stays flat. The human still does all contextual work. When output disappoints, people blame themselves, but Johnson insists the mismatch is the interface, not the user: we shortcut the interface in the race to enable AI.

sections.title: Personal Plex: Real-Time Conversation Demonstration
sections.summary: Johnson shows Nvidia's Personal Plex handling interruptions, topic changes (diet to marathon), yielding, picking threads back up, and backchanneling naturally. He notes making listening noises is not the same as knowing who is in the room, and that models are not trained to distinguish speech meant for them. Frontier work is improving the protocol to give models better understanding of human and group conversation.

sections.title: Business Meeting Scenario: Participatory AI in Action
sections.summary: Johnson demonstrates a multi-person business meeting where AI tracks participants (Sam, Jordan), labels statements as questions or proposals, holds context across turns, resolves a scope objective about expense approvals versus access requests, captures decisions, answers a room-availability question, and takes actions only when no one else is holding the floor. No one wrote or submitted a prompt; the system participated in the conversation and chose its moment.

sections.title: The Mindset Shift: AI as Interface Technology
sections.summary: Johnson delivers his closing argument: AI is increasingly an interface technology, not just an intelligence technology. Stop picturing AI as a smarter machine behind prompts; start seeing intelligence as something that can remove interface constraints. For 75 years humans adapted to the machine. The design question becomes what burden we still place on humans only because machines used to be too limited. The answer is the affordances humans already use—questions, pauses, sketches, checklists, quiet asides, or saying nothing. Computing has been about improving how humans encode intent; each step carried old constraints forward as translation, precision, context, and repair taxes. AI is the chance to put those down.
